description.sr_latin: Fraze za slavlja, zdravice, rođendane, slavu i druženje.
description.en: Phrases for celebrations, toasts, birthdays, slava, and gathering culture.

phrases.context: Everyone's glass is raised around the table — what do you say as you clink?
phrases.notes: Literally means 'may we live'. Always look people in the eyes when you say it.

phrases.context: Glasses are up and you want to toast to everyone's good health rather than just say cheers.
phrases.notes: You can specify whose health: 'U tvoje zdravlje!' = 'To your health!'

phrases.context: Someone next to you just sneezed — say the little blessing (it doubles as a toast).
phrases.notes: One of the most versatile phrases. Context determines the meaning.

phrases.context: Just you and your partner clinking glasses on a date — make the toast about the two of you.
phrases.notes: Short and sweet. Very common between couples.

phrases.context: You walk in and hand your friend their gift on their big day — what do you say first?
phrases.notes: 'Rođendan' literally = 'birth day'. 'Srećan' = happy/fortunate.

phrases.context: You've just wished a happy birthday and want to add a warm second line — wish them everything good.
phrases.notes: 'Najbolje' = the best (superlative of 'dobro'). Very common well-wish.

phrases.context: Glasses up for the birthday guy — shout the 'hip hip hooray' cheer straight at him.
phrases.notes: For a woman: 'Živela!' For a group: 'Živeli!'

phrases.context: Asking someone what age they're celebrating.
phrases.notes: 'Puniti godine' = to turn (an age). More natural than 'Koliko imaš godina?' in a birthday context.

phrases.context: You arrive at a family's patron-saint feast — what do you say as you step through the door?
phrases.notes: Slava is a uniquely Serbian tradition — each family celebrates their patron saint annually. It's UNESCO-protected. This is the most important thing to know.

phrases.sr_latin: Da Bog da slavili još mnogo godina!
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Да Бог да славили још много година!
phrases.en: God willing, may you celebrate for many more years!
phrases.context: A traditional wish at someone's slava. Shows respect for the tradition.
phrases.notes: 'Da Bog da' = 'God willing' / 'may God grant'. Very traditional phrasing.

phrases.context: Asking someone about their family's patron saint day. This shows genuine interest in Serbian culture.
phrases.notes: Every Serbian family has one. Asking this is a great conversation starter and shows you care.

phrases.context: Asking which saint the family celebrates. Common saints: Sveti Nikola, Sveti Sava, Sveti Đorđe.
phrases.notes: 'Vaša' (your, formal/plural) because you're asking about the whole family's tradition.

phrases.context: The clock strikes midnight on December 31st — what do you say to everyone around you?
phrases.notes: Serbs celebrate both Jan 1 (New Year) and Jan 14 (Orthodox New Year / 'Srpska Nova godina').

phrases.context: Serbian Orthodox Christmas greeting (January 7th). The response is 'Vaistinu se rodi!'
phrases.notes: Even non-religious Serbs use this. Christmas is Jan 7, not Dec 25.

phrases.context: You're leaving the office before the holiday break — wish everyone well without naming a specific day.
phrases.notes: 'Praznici' = holidays (plural of 'praznik').

phrases.context: Everyone's glass is empty and the night is young — push for another round.
phrases.notes: 'Ajmo' = colloquial 'hajdemo' (let's go). 'Još jednu' = one more (feminine, referring to 'čašu' — glass).

phrases.en: Nothing will happen to you, drink!
phrases.context: What your Serbian friends say when you try to stop drinking. Peer pressure, but affectionate.
phrases.notes: 'Pij' = drink (imperative). This is the classic Serbian encouragement.

phrases.sr_latin: Dosta mi je, ne mogu više.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Доста ми је, не могу више.
phrases.en: I've had enough, I can't anymore.
phrases.context: Trying to stop drinking. Good luck — they probably won't accept this.
phrases.notes: 'Dosta' = enough. 'Ne mogu više' = I can't anymore. Expect to hear 'Ma daj, još jednu!'

phrases.context: Serbs are proud of their homemade rakija. Expect this announcement before every pour.
phrases.notes: 'Domaća' = homemade. Homemade rakija is a point of family pride — always compliment it. 'Rakija' comes from Turkish 'rakı'.

phrases.context: Guests have arrived and you're opening the door for them — what's the first thing you say?
phrases.notes: Literally 'well come'. For one person: 'Dobro došao!' (m) / 'Dobro došla!' (f).

phrases.en: Take your shoes off, make yourself at home.
phrases.context: Asking guests to remove shoes. Standard in Serbian homes.
phrases.notes: 'Izuti se' = to take off shoes. 'Slobodno' = freely/feel free. You'll get house slippers ('papuče').

phrases.sr_latin: Jesi gladan? Imam da ti ponudim nešto.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Јеси гладан? Имам да ти понудим нешто.
phrases.en: Are you hungry? I have something to offer you.
phrases.context: A Serbian host will ALWAYS offer food. Refusing is almost impossible.
phrases.notes: For a female guest: 'Jesi gladna?' Serbian hospitality means you will be fed whether you want to or not.

variations.sr_latin: Jesi gladna? Imam da ti ponudim nešto.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Јеси гладна? Имам да ти понудим нешто.
variations.en: Are you hungry? I have something to offer you.

phrases.en: Feel at home. / Make yourself at home.
phrases.context: Telling someone to relax and feel comfortable in your space.
phrases.notes: 'Kod kuće' = at home. 'Osećaj se' = feel yourself (imperative, reflexive).

phrases.context: Asking about plans for going out.
phrases.notes: 'Žurka' = party (informal). 'Večeras' = tonight.

phrases.context: Checking how late the night is going to go. The answer is usually 'until morning'.
phrases.notes: 'Do kad' = until when. Spoiler: there is rarely a firm end time.

phrases.context: Complimenting the music at a gathering or party.
phrases.notes: 'Odlična' = excellent (feminine, matching 'muzika'). Serbs take their music seriously.

phrases.context: When the party energy is rising. Classic request.
phrases.notes: 'Pojačati' = to turn up/amplify. Opposite: 'Smanji muziku' (turn it down).

phrases.context: Inviting friends over. Serbian socializing often happens at someone's home.
phrases.notes: 'Kod mene' = at my place. Very casual and spontaneous — this is how plans happen.

phrases.sr_latin: Dolazi, nemoj da se praviš važan.
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Долази, немој да се правиш важан.
phrases.en: Come on, don't act all important.
phrases.context: Pressuring a friend who's trying to bail on plans. Said with love.
phrases.notes: 'Praviti se važan' = to act important/busy. Feminine: 'važna'. Classic guilt-trip among friends.

variations.sr_latin: Dolazi, nemoj da se praviš važna.
variations.sr_cyrillic: Долази, немој да се правиш важна.
variations.en: Come on, don't act all important.

phrases.context: Organizing who brings food/drinks to a gathering.
phrases.notes: Short and efficient. The answer is usually 'Ja donosim piće' (I'm bringing drinks) or 'Ja donosim meze' (I'm bringing snacks).

phrases.en: No worries, come whenever you can.
phrases.context: Telling people there's no rush, come when they're ready. Very Serbian approach to timing.
phrases.notes: 'Nema frke' = no worries/no stress (slang). 'Kad stignete' = when you manage to arrive.

phrases.context: Your friend just told you they passed their driving test — congratulate them.
phrases.notes: 'Čestitati' = to congratulate. Can add what for: 'Čestitam ti na...' (I congratulate you on...).

phrases.context: A friend pulled off something genuinely impressive — tip your hat to them.
phrases.notes: Literally 'every honor'. Used constantly in casual speech. Works for big and small achievements.

phrases.context: Telling your partner or friend you're proud of them.
phrases.notes: Feminine: 'Ponosna sam na tebe!' Deeply meaningful in close relationships.

phrases.context: Your partner announces they got a raise — react by insisting this calls for a celebration.
phrases.notes: 'Proslaviti' = to celebrate. Serbs will find a reason to celebrate almost anything.

phrases.context: Announcing your departure. Expect resistance and at least 30 more minutes of saying goodbye.
phrases.notes: 'Ljudi' = people/guys. Adding it makes the goodbye casual and warm.

phrases.en: Where are you going? It's early!
phrases.context: What everyone says when you try to leave. Even at 3 AM, it's apparently 'early'.
phrases.notes: 'Gde ćeš' = where are you going (literally 'where will you'). Standard protest when someone tries to leave.

phrases.sr_latin: Bilo je odlično, hvala na svemu!
phrases.sr_cyrillic: Било је одлично, хвала на свему!
phrases.en: It was great, thanks for everything!
phrases.context: Thanking your host when you finally manage to leave.
phrases.notes: 'Hvala na svemu' = thanks for everything. A warm and proper way to end the evening.

phrases.context: A casual goodbye that keeps the connection going.
phrases.notes: 'Vidimo se' = we see each other / see you. 'Uskoro' = soon.
